\begin{example}\label{ExEvenEq}
Consider the \egtrs{} $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$, 
where
%
$\Symbols=\{\arityOf{\fS{0}}{0},\arityOf{\fS{odd}}{1},\arityOf{\fS{pev}}{1},
\linebreak
\arityOf{\fS{s}}{1},\arityOf{\fS{test}}{1},\arityOf{\fS{zero}}{1}\}$,
%
$\SPredicates=\{\arityOf{\fS{\geq}}{2},\arityOf{\ceq}{2},\arityOf{{\rew{}}}{2},\arityOf{{\rews{}}}{2}\}$,
%
$\mu=\muTop$,
%
$E=\{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})\}$,
%
$H=\{(\ref{ExEvenEq_clause1}),(\ref{ExEvenEq_clause2})\}$,
and
$R=\{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1}),(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule2}),(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule3})\}$.
%
\begin{eqnarray}
\fS{s}(\fS{s}(x)) &\ceq  & x  \IF x\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_eq1}
\\
x & \geq & 0\label{ExEvenEq_clause1}
\\
\fS{s}(x) & \geq & \fS{s}(y) \IF x\geq y\label{ExEvenEq_clause2}
\\
\fS{test}(x) & \to & \fS{pev}(x)\IF x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0}))\label{ExEvenEq_rule1}
\\
\fS{test}(x) & \to & \fS{odd}(x)\IF x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_rule2}
\\
\fS{test}(x) & \to & \fS{zero}(x)\IF x\ceq\fS{0}\label{ExEvenEq_rule3}
\end{eqnarray}
where 
$\geq$ is defined by the Horn clauses (\ref{ExEvenEq_clause1}) and (\ref{ExEvenEq_clause2}).
%
Rules (\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1}), (\ref{ExEvenEq_rule2}), and (\ref{ExEvenEq_rule3}) define tests to check
whether a number (in Peano notation) is either
\emph{positive and even}, \emph{odd} or \emph{zero} using the equivalence specified by (\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1}).
%
We obtain the following conditional pairs:
\begin{eqnarray}
\ccpOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1}),\toppos,(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule2})}: 
&& \langle\fS{odd}(x),\fS{pev}(x)\rangle\IF x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0})),x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_CCP1}
\\
\ccpOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1}),\toppos,(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule3})}: 
&& \langle\fS{zero}(x),\fS{pev}(x)\rangle\IF x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0})),x\ceq\fS{0}\label{ExEvenEq_CCP2}
\\
\ccpOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule2}),\toppos,(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule3})}: 
&& \langle\fS{zero}(x),\fS{odd}(x)\rangle\IF x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{0}),x\ceq\fS{0}\label{ExEvenEq_CCP3}
\\
\cvpROf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1}),x,1}: 
&& \langle\fS{test}(x'),\fS{pev}(x)\rangle\IF x\rew{}x',x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0}))\label{ExEvenEq_CVP1}
\\
\cvpROf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule2}),x,1}: 
&& \langle\fS{test}(x'),\fS{odd}(x)\rangle\IF x\rew{}x',x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_CVP2}
\\
\cvpROf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule3}),x,1}: 
&& \langle\fS{test}(x'),\fS{zero}(x)\rangle\IF x\rew{}x',x\ceq\fS{0}\label{ExEvenEq_CVP3}
\\
\ccpOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1}),\toppos,\overleftarrow{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})}}:
&& \langle\fS{s}(\fS{s}(x)),\fS{pev}(x)\rangle \IF x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0})),\fS{test}(x)\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_RECCP1}
\\
\ccpOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule2}),\toppos,\overleftarrow{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})}}:
&& \langle\fS{s}(\fS{s}(x)),\fS{odd}(x)\rangle \IF x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{0}),\fS{test}(x)\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_RECCP2}
\\
\ccpOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule3}),\toppos,\overleftarrow{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})}}:
&& \langle\fS{s}(\fS{s}(x)),\fS{zero}(x)\rangle \IF x\ceq\fS{0},\fS{test}(x)\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_RECCP3}
\\
\cvpROf{\overrightarrow{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})},x,1.1}: 
&& \langle\fS{s}(\fS{s}(x')),x\rangle\IF x\rew{}x',x\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_ECVP1}
\\
\cvpROf{\overleftarrow{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})},x,1.1}: 
&& \langle x',\fS{s}(\fS{s}(x))\rangle\IF x\rew{}x',x\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_ECVP2}
\\
\cvpEqOneOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1}),x,1}: 
&& \langle\fS{test}(x'),\fS{pev}(x)\rangle\IF x\equone{}x',x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0}))\label{ExEvenEq_RECVP1}
\\
\cvpEqOneOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule2}),x,1}: 
&& \langle\fS{test}(x'),\fS{odd}(x)\rangle\IF x\equone{}x',x\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{0})\label{ExEvenEq_RECVP2}
\\
\cvpEqOneOf{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule3}),x,1}: 
&& \langle\fS{test}(x'),\fS{zero}(x)\rangle\IF x\equone{}x',x\ceq\fS{0}\label{ExEvenEq_RECVP3}
\end{eqnarray}
%
We have: 
%
\begin{itemize}
\item $\CCP(\cR)=\emptyset$,
as all CCPs (\ref{ExEvenEq_CCP1}), (\ref{ExEvenEq_CCP2}), and (\ref{ExEvenEq_CCP3}) are \emph{infeasible} and
no iCCP is considered, as all rules in $R$ are 2-rules.
%
\item $\CVPofR(\cR)=\emptyset$, as the CVPs (\ref{ExEvenEq_CVP1}),(\ref{ExEvenEq_CVP2}), and (\ref{ExEvenEq_CVP3}) are all \emph{infeasible}: terms $s$ which can be rewritten with $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$ cannot be proved equivalent to 
$\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0}))$, $\fS{s}(\fS{0})$ or $\fS{0}$, 
i.e., $s\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0}))$, $s\ceq\fS{s}(\fS{0})$, and $s\ceq\fS{0}$ cannot be proved. 
%
Indeed, if $s$ can be rewritten with $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$, at least a subterm $\fS{test}(s')$ is inside $s$ for some term $s'$. 
%
Since symbols $\fS{test}$ are not removed but just replaced by $\fS{pev}$, $\fS{odd}$, or $\fS{zero}$, no $\equequ{E}$-match with a term 
$\fS{s}^n(\fS{0})$ is possible for any $n\geq 0$. 
%
\item $\CCP(E,\cR)=\emptyset$, as there is no rule in $R$ overlaps a rule in $\eqoriented{E}$.
%
\item $\CCP(\cR,E)=\emptyset$
is empty because the CCPs (\ref{ExEvenEq_RECCP1}),(\ref{ExEvenEq_RECCP2}), and (\ref{ExEvenEq_RECCP3})
are all infeasible, 
as the condition $\fS{test}(x)\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})$, which occurs in all of them, is not satisfiable.
%
\item $\CVPofR(E)=\emptyset$ as the CVPs (\ref{ExEvenEq_ECVP1}) and (\ref{ExEvenEq_ECVP2}) are \emph{infeasible}: terms $s$ which can be rewritten with $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$ cannot be compared with $\fS{s}(\fS{0})$ using $\geq$, i.e., $s\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})$ cannot be proved.
%
\item $\CVPofEqOne(\cR)=\{(\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP1}),(\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP2}),(\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP3})\}$, consists of
$\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinable CVPs.
%
For instance, consider (\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP1}): if $s\equone{E}t$ holds for some terms $s$ and $t$, then either 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $s\rew{\overrightarrow{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})}}t$ (hence $s=\fS{s}(\fS{s}(t))$)
and $t\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})$ holds; furthermore, 
$s\equequ{E}\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0}))$ also holds.
%
This implies that $s=\fS{s}^{2n}(\fS{0})$ for some $n> 1$
and $t=\fS{s}^{2n-2}(\fS{0})$.
%
Since $n>1$, $2n-2\geq 2$, we have
$\fS{test}(t)\rew{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1})}\fS{pev}(t)\equone{E}\fS{pev}(s)$, i.e., (\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP1}) is $\lsejoinability{\cR}$-joinable, hence $\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinable.
%
\item Dually, if $s\rew{\overleftarrow{(\ref{ExEvenEq_eq1})}}t$ (hence $t=\fS{s}(\fS{s}(s))$)
and $s\geq\fS{s}(\fS{0})$ holds; furthermore, 
$s\equequ{E}\fS{s}(\fS{s}(\fS{0}))$ also holds.
%
This implies that $s=\fS{s}^{2n}(\fS{0})$ for some $n>0$
and $t=\fS{s}^{2n+2}(\fS{0})$.
%
Since $n\geq 0$, $2n+2\geq 2$ and
$\fS{test}(t)\rew{(\ref{ExEvenEq_rule1})}\fS{pev}(t)\equone{E}\fS{pev}(s)$, i.e., (\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP1}) is $\lsejoinability{\cR}$-joinable, hence $\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinable.
\end{enumerate}
For (\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP2}) and (\ref{ExEvenEq_RECVP3}), we 
reason similarly
to conclude their $\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinability.
\end{itemize}
Overall, Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_EConfluence}) proves $E$-confluence of $\cR$ (which is clearly $E$-terminating).
\end{example}
%
As a corollary of Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_EConfluence}) 
and our previous results on joinability of CVPs, 
we give syntactic conditions on \egtrs{s} showing that 
only CCPs need to be proved $\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinable to conclude $E$-confluence.

\begin{corollary}
\label{CoroEConfluenceOfETerminatingLeftLinearEGTRSsHuet}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an \egtrs{}
such that $R^\RMabbr$ is $\mu$-left-linear and $\mu$-compatible
and $\eqoriented{E}$ is left-$\mu$-homogeneous and $\mu$-compatible.
%
If $\cR$ is $E$-terminating, then it is $E$-confluent if all pairs in 
$\CCP(\cR) 
\cup\CCP(E,\cR)\cup\CCP(\cR,E)
$
are $\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinable.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Due to $\mu$-left-linearity 
(which implies $\mu$-homogeneity) 
and $\mu$-compatibility 
of rules in $R^\RMabbr$, 
by Corollary \ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForCriticalVariablesNotInCond}
and Corollary \ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks}(\ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks_CVPeq}), the CVPs in $\CVPofR(\cR)\cup\CVPofEqOne(\cR)$ are $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr}$-joinable.
%
Due to left-$\mu$-homogeneity 
and $\mu$-compatibility 
of rules in $\eqoriented{E}$, by Corollary \ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks}(\ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks_CVPto}), the CVPs in $\CVPofR(E)$ are $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr}$-joinable.
%
By Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_EConfluence}), $\cR$ is $E$-confluent.
\end{proof}
%
\noindent
Note the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item  Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_EqCCPsAndEqCVPs} shows that we \emph{cannot prove} $E$-confluence of $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_EGTRS} by using Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_EConfluence}) 
or Corollary \ref{CoroEConfluenceOfETerminatingLeftLinearEGTRSsHuet}
as $\cR$ is not 
left-linear and the CVPs in 
$\CVPofEqOne(\cR)$ are \emph{not} $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr}$-joinable,
although they are $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable.
%
\item Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_CCPsAndCVPs}
shows that we \emph{cannot disprove} $E$-confluence of $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs} (witnessed by the peak $\fS{d}\leftrew{\cR,E}\fS{f}(\fS{c})\rew{\cR}\fS{f}(\fS{d})$, which is not $\ejoinability{\cR/E}$-joinable) by using Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_NonEConfluent}), as $\CCP(\cR)=\CVPofR(\cR)=\emptyset$.
\end{enumerate}
%
The use of Jouannaud and Kirchner's notions of 
\emph{local confluence modulo $E$ of $\rew{\cR,E}$ with $\rew{\cR}$} 
and
\emph{local coherence modulo $E$ of $\rew{\cR,E}$} 
permits to obtain $E$-confluence criteria exploiting $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinability of conditional pairs.

\medskip
\noindent
In the following, we develop this approach,  which permits to solve the two aforementioned open problems.
%
A proof of $E$-confluence of $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_EGTRS} is given 
in Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_EConfluence}.
%
Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_notEconfluent} proves that $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs} is not $E$-confluent.

\section{Analysis of $\cR^\RMabbr,E$-reduction and coherence peaks}
\label{SecAnalysisOfPSRandCpeaks}

In this section, we consider the shape of PS-r-peaks (\ref{LblAbstractRPeakJK86})
and 
PS-c-peaks (\ref{LblAbstractCPeakJK86}).

\subsection{$\cR^\RMabbr,E$-reduction peaks}

Given an \egtrs{} $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ 
and \emph{terms} $s$, $t$, and $t'$ defining a PS-r-peak (\ref{LblAbstractRPeakJK86}), i.e.,
%
\[t\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}  s  \rew{\cR^\RMabbr} t',\]
%
by Proposition \ref{PropUseOfRulesAndPositionsInRewritingSteps_EGTRSs}(\ref{PropUseOfRulesAndPositionsInRewritingSteps_EGTRSs_PStickel}) 
there are active positions $\ol{p},\ol{p'}\in\Pos^\mu(s)$,
%
rules $\alpha:\lhsr\to\rhsr\IF\gencond,\alpha':\lhsr'\to\rhsr'\IF\gencond'\in R^\RMabbr$
sharing no variable, 
and
substitution $\sigma$,
such that 
(i) $s|_{\ol{p}}=w=_E\sigma(\lhsr)$ and $\sigma(\gencond)$ hold; 
and 
(ii) $s|_{\ol{p'}}=\sigma(\lhsr')$ and $\sigma(\gencond')$ hold, i.e.,
every rewriting peak is of the form
\begin{eqnarray}
t = s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}}~ \leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E} ~ s[\underleftarrow{w}]_{\ol{p}}~~=& s & =~~s[\underrightarrow{\sigma(\lhsr')}]_{\ol{p'}} ~\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}~ s[\sigma(\rhsr')]_{\ol{p'}}=t'\label{GenericRPeakTermsJK86}
\end{eqnarray}
%
Note from Table \ref{TableJoinabilityOfRpeaksJK86}, that PS-r-peaks are required to be $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable.

\subsubsection{Classes of PS-r-peaks}
%
Depending on the relative location of $\ol{p}$ and $\ol{p'}$, 
different classes of peaks (\ref{GenericRPeakTermsJK86}) are
distinguished. 

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{\emph{Disjoint} PS-r-peaks.}
%
If $\ol{p}$ and $\ol{p'}$ in (\ref{GenericRPeakTermsJK86})
are \emph{disjoint}, i.e., $\ol{p}\parallel \ol{p'}$, 
then $s=s[w]_{\ol{p}}[\sigma'(\lhsr')]_{\ol{p'}}=s[\sigma'(\lhsr')]_{\ol{p'}}[w]_{\ol{p}}$. 
Accordingly, (\ref{GenericRPeakTermsJK86}) can be written as follows:
\begin{eqnarray}
t = s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}} [\sigma(\lhsr')]_{\ol{p'}} \leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}    & 
s[\underleftarrow{w}]_{\ol{p}}[\underrightarrow{\sigma(\lhsr')}]_{\ol{p'}} 
& 
\rew{\cR^\RMabbr} 
s[w]_{\ol{p}}[\sigma(\rhsr')]_{\ol{p'}}  = t'
~~~\label{DisjointRPeakTerms}
\end{eqnarray}
Since
$
t = s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}} [\underrightarrow{\sigma(\lhsr')}]_{\ol{p'}} ~\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}~ 
s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}} [\sigma(\rhsr')]_{\ol{p'}} 
~\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}~ s[\underleftarrow{w}]_{\ol{p}}[\sigma(\rhsr')]_{\ol{p'}}  = t'
$,
$t$ and $t'$ are $\joinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-\emph{joinable}.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{\emph{Nested} PS-r-peaks.}\label{SecNestedEPeaks}
%
If $\ol{p'}=\ol{p}.p\in\Pos^\mu(s)$ for $\ol{p}$ and $\ol{p'}$ in (\ref{GenericRPeakTermsJK86})
and some position $p$, then (\ref{GenericRPeakTermsJK86})
can be written in one of the following possibilities, according to 
the position 
where the $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$-step applies
 (by abuse, we also use $t$ and $t'$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item In the first case, rewriting with $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$ occurs \emph{above or on} the $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-step and
we have
% as
\begin{eqnarray}
t = \sigma(\lhsr)[\sigma(\rhsr')]_p ~\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}   & \underrightarrow{\sigma(\lhsr)[\overleftarrow{w}]_p} & \rew{\cR^\RMabbr}~\sigma(\rhsr)=t'\label{NestedPSRupPeak}
%
\end{eqnarray}
%
where $w=_E\sigma(\lhsr')$ and $p\geq\toppos$.
We call  (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) a \emph{PS-r-up-peak}.
%
We distinguish two cases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $p\in\Pos^\mu_\Symbols(\lhsr)$, then $\sigma(\lhsr)|_p=\sigma(\lhsr|_p)=w=_E\sigma(\lhsr')$, i.e.,
$\lhsr'$ and $\lhsr|_p$ $E$-unify. Then, we say that
(\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) is a \emph{critical PS-r-up-peak}; 
\item If $p\notin\Pos^\mu_\Symbols(\lhsr)$, there is $x\in\Var^\mu(\lhsr)$ 
and $q\in\Pos^\mu(\lhsr)$ such that $\lhsr|_q=x$ and $q\leq p$.
Then, we say
that (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) is a \emph{variable PS-r-up-peak}.
\end{enumerate}
%
\item In the second case, rewriting with $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$ occurs \emph{below} the $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-step;
we have
\begin{eqnarray}
t =  \sigma(\rhsr')~\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}   & \overleftarrow{w[\underrightarrow{\sigma(\lhsr)}]_p} & \rew{\cR^\RMabbr}~w[\sigma(\rhsr)]_p=t'\label{NestedPSRdownPeak}
\end{eqnarray}
%
where $w=w[\sigma(\lhsr')]_p=_E\sigma(\lhsr)$ and $p>\toppos$, 
as $p=\toppos$ coincide with $p=\toppos$ in (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}).
We call  (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak}) a \emph{PS-r-down peak}. 
\end{enumerate}
%
\begin{remark}[Critical and variable PS-r-down-peaks?]
\label{RemRupAndRdownPeaksIfEisEmpty}
We do not distinguish between critical and variable PS-r-down-peaks: due to the use $E$-matching in $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-steps, it is not possible to qualify position $p$, where the $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$-step using $\alpha$ occurs, as ``overlapping'' (or not) rule $\alpha'$ which is used in the $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-step.
\end{remark}
%
Proposition \ref{PropJoinableVariablePeaksForCriticalVariablesNotInCondition} 
has a counterpart for
PS-r-up-peaks; the proof is analogous.

\begin{proposition}[Joinable variable PS-r-up-peaks]
\label{PropJoinableVariablePSrUpPeaksForCriticalVariablesNotInCondition}
A variable PS-r-up-peak (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) is 
$\lsjoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable 
if 
$\alpha$ is left-$\mu$-homogeneous and $\mu$-compatible.
%
Furthermore, if $x\in\Var^\mu(\rhsr)$, then (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) is 
$\sjoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable.
\end{proposition}

Given an \egtrs{} $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$, 
critical  PS-r-peaks  (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) are captured by different kinds of conditional pairs as follows.

\paragraph{Critical PS-r-up-peaks} 
In contrast to critical r-peaks, which are treated by means of CCPs (Section \ref{SecConditionalPairsForNestedRpeaks}), 
critical PS-r-up-peaks (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) are captured by LCCPs (Figure \ref{FigPSrUpPeakAndLCCP}) 
as follows:
%
\[\LCCP(\cR)  =  \GLCCP(R^\showRMabbr,R^\showRMabbr)
\]

\begin{proposition}[Critical PS-r-up-peaks and LCCPs]
\label{PropCriticalPSrUpPeaksAndConditionalCriticalPairs}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an \egtrs{}. 
Let $\alpha:\lhsr\to\rhsr\IF\gencond,\alpha':\lhsr'\to\rhsr'\IF\gencond'\in R^\RMabbr$,
sharing no variable, induce 
critical PS-r-up-peaks (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) 
with $p\in\Pos^\mu_\Symbols(\lhsr')$ 
as in (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}).
%
Then, (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) is $\joinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable 
($\joinability{\cR/E}$-joinable), iff
$\pi_{\alpha,p,\alpha'}
\in\LCCP(\cR)$ is $\joinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable ($\joinability{\cR^\RMabbr/E}$-joinable).
\end{proposition}
%
\begin{proof}
Let (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}) be
\[\begin{array}{rcl}
t = \sigma(\lhsr)[\sigma(\rhsr')]_p ~\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}   & \underrightarrow{\sigma(\lhsr)[\overleftarrow{w}]_p} & \rew{\cR^\RMabbr}~\sigma(\rhsr)=t'
\end{array}
\]
where
$p\in\Pos^\mu_\Symbols(\lhsr)$ and $\sigma(\gencond)$ and $\sigma(\gencond')$ are 
satisfied, and $\pi_{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$ is 
$\langle\lhsr[\rhsr']_p,\rhsr\rangle\IF \lhsr|_p=\lhsr',\gencond,\gencond'$.
%
Since $\sigma(\lhsr)|_p=\sigma(\lhsr|_p)=w=_E\sigma(\lhsr')$ in (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}),
$\sigma$ is also an $E$-unifier of $\lhsr|_p$ and $\lhsr'$.
%
Hence, $\sigma$ satisfies the conditional part of $\pi_{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$.
%
By $\cR^\RMabbr,E$-joinability  (resp.\ $\cR/E$-joinable) of (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}), $\pi_{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$
is also $\cR^\RMabbr,E$-joinable  (resp.\ $\cR/E$-joinable), as $\sigma$ is not restricted in any way.
%
Vice versa: every substitution $\sigma$ satisfying the conditional part of $\pi_{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$ can also be used to define a peak (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak}), which is
$\cR^\RMabbr,E$-joinable (resp.\ $\cR/E$-joinable), if $\pi_{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$ is $\cR^\RMabbr,E$-joinable (resp.\ $\cR/E$-joinable).
\end{proof}
%%
As for CCPs, $\LCCP(\cR)=\pLCCP(\cR)\uplus\iLCCP(\cR)$, where $\pLCCP(\cR)$ (resp.\ $\iLCCP(\cR)$) consists of all feasible 
\emph{proper} (resp.\ \emph{improper}) LCCPs. 
%
Improper LCCPs 
of 2-rules 
are also trivial.
%
Thus, we can drop all iLCCPs $\ilccpOf{\alpha}$ of 2-rules $\alpha$ from $\LCCP(\cR)$.

(see Remark \ref{RemRefiningCCPR}).

The following result is useful to analyze joinability of LCCPs (as infeasibility).
%
Here, given a set of rules $S$, $\DSymbols(S)=\{\rootTerm(\alhsr)\mid \alhsr\to\arhsr\IF\agencond\in S\}$ is the set of function symbols \emph{defined} by means of some rule in the usual sense.
%
Also, we say that a rule $\alhsr\to\arhsr\IF\agencond$ is \emph{collapsing} if $\arhsr$ is a variable (cf. \cite[Definition 9.2.3]{BaaNip_TermRewritingAndAllThat_1998}).

\begin{proposition}
\label{PropInfeasibilityOfLCCPsWithEqCondWithNoEqSymbol}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an \egtrs{}, 
$\alpha:\lhsr\to\rhsr\IF\gencond,\alpha':\lhsr'\to\rhsr'\IF\gencond'\in R^\showRMabbr$ 
and $\lccpOf{\alpha,p,\alpha'} \in\LCCP(\cR)$ be such that $\rootTree(\lhsr|_p)
\notin\DSymbols(\eqoriented{E})$
and $\rootTree(\lhsr|_p)\neq\rootTree(\lhsr')$.
If 
(i) $\eqoriented{E}$ is \emph{not} collapsing, or
(ii) $\rootTree(\lhsr')\notin\DSymbols(\eqoriented{E})$,
then $\lccpOf{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$ is 
infeasible.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By definition of LCCP, since $p\in\Pos^\mu_\Symbols(\lhsr)$ 
and 
$\alpha'\in R^\showRMabbr$, 
we have $\lhsr|_p,\lhsr'\notin\Variables$.
%
If $\sigma$ satisfies $\lhsr|_p=\lhsr'$,
then, 
\begin{eqnarray}
\sigma(\lhsr|_p)\rews{\eqoriented{E}}\sigma(\lhsr')\label{PropInfeasibilityOfLCCPsWithEqCondWithNoEqSymbol_Sequence}
\end{eqnarray}
%
Note that $\rootTree(\lhsr|_p)\neq\rootTree(\lhsr')$ and $\rootTree(\lhsr|_p)\notin\DSymbols(\eqoriented{E})$.
In case (i), reductions with $\rew{\eqoriented{E}}$ are not applied at the root and cannot change 
$\rootTree(\sigma(\lhsr|_p))$, which is $\rootTree(\lhsr|_p)$.
Since $\lhsr'$ is not a variable and $\rootTree(\sigma(\lhsr'))=\rootTree(\lhsr')\neq\rootTree(\lhsr|_p)$, sequence (\ref{PropInfeasibilityOfLCCPsWithEqCondWithNoEqSymbol_Sequence}) is not possible.
Thus, $\lccpOf{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$ is 
infeasible.
%
In case (ii), even if a rule $x\to t\in\eqoriented{E}$ is applied for some variable $x$, $\rootTree(t)\in\DSymbols(\eqoriented{E})$ and $t$ could not be rewritten to $\sigma(\lhsr')$ whose root symbol $\rootTree(\lhsr')$ is not in $\DSymbols(\eqoriented{E})$. Thus, $\lccpOf{\alpha,p,\alpha'}$ is 
infeasible.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Down conditional pairs]
\label{DefDownConditionalPair}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an \egtrs{}.
%
Rule  $\alpha:\lhsr\to\rhsr\IF\gencond\in R^\RMabbr$ 
defines a \emph{Down Conditional Pair} (DCP for short) as follows:
\begin{eqnarray}
\dcpOf{\alpha}: \langle \rhsr,x'\rangle\IF x\ceq\lhsr,x\innerrew{} x',\gencond\label{LblDownConditionalCriticalPair}
\end{eqnarray}
%
where $x$ and $x'$ are fresh variables.
The set of feasible DCPs obtained in this way 
$\DCP(\cR)$. 
\end{definition}
%
In Definition \ref{DefDownConditionalPair}, predicate symbol $\innerrew{}$
refers to \emph{inner} (i.e., \emph{non-root}) $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$-rewriting steps.
%
As usual, $\innerrew{}$ is defined by deduction on $\crtheoryOf{\cR}$ extended with the theory 
%
\begin{eqnarray}
\{\RuleInnerRed_{f,i,\alpha}\mid f\in\Symbols,i\in\mu(f),\alpha\in R^\RMabbr\}
\cup
\{(\RulePropagation)^{\innerrew{}}_{f,i}\mid f\in\Symbols,i\in\mu(f)\}
\end{eqnarray}
%
where sentences 
%
$\RuleInnerRed_{f,i,\alpha}$ for rules 
$\alpha:\lhsr\to\rhsr\IF A_1,\ldots,A_n$
are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
 (\forall\vec{x}\vec{y})A_1\wedge\cdots \wedge A_n\Rightarrow f(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},\lhsr,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_k)\innerrew{}f(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},\rhsr,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_k)
\end{array}
\]
where 
$\vec{x}$, i.e., $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ are fresh, pairwise distinct variables,
which are not in $\vec{y}$, the variables occurring in $\alpha$.

\begin{proposition}[PS-r-down peaks and DCPs]
\label{PropRdownPeaksAndDownConditionalCriticalPairs}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an \egtrs{}. 
Let $\alpha:\lhsr\to\rhsr\IF\gencond,\alpha':\lhsr'\to\rhsr'\IF\gencond'\in R^\RMabbr$,
sharing no variable, determine 
PS-r-down peaks (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak}).
%
Then, (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak}) is 
$\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable  ($\ejoinability{\cR/E}$-joinable) iff
$\pi_{\alpha}
\in\DCP(\cR)$ is $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable  ($\ejoinability{\cR/E}$-joinable).  
\end{proposition}
%
\begin{proof}
Let (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak}) be 
\[\begin{array}{rcl}
t =  \sigma(\rhsr)~\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}   & \overleftarrow{w[\underrightarrow{\sigma(\lhsr')}]_p} & \rew{\cR^\RMabbr}~w[\sigma(\rhsr')]_p=t'
\end{array}
\]
where 
%
$p>\toppos$ and $\sigma(\gencond)$ and $\sigma(\gencond')$ are 
satisfied, and 
$\pi_{\alpha}$ is $\langle \rhsr,x'\rangle\IF x\ceq\lhsr,x\innerrew{} x',\gencond$.

As for the \emph{only if} part, since $w=w[\sigma(\lhsr')]_p=_E\sigma(\lhsr)$, and $x,x'\notin\Var(\alpha,\alpha')$, we can let $\sigma(x)=w[\sigma(\lhsr')]_p$ and $\sigma(x')=w[\sigma(\rhsr')]_p$.
%
Hence, the conditional part of $\pi_{\alpha,\alpha'}$ is satisfied by $\sigma$.
%
By $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinability of (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak}), $\pi_{\alpha}$
is also $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable (and hence $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr/E}$-joinable).

As for the \emph{if} part, let $\sigma$ be a substitution satisfying the conditional part of 
$\pi_{\alpha}$.
%
In particular, $\sigma(x)=_E\sigma(\lhsr)$ holds and, since $\sigma(\gencond)$ also  holds,  we have $\sigma(x)\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}\sigma(\rhsr)=t$.
%
We also have $\sigma(x)\innerrew{\cR^\RMabbr}\sigma(x')$, i.e.,
$\sigma(x)=w[\sigma(\lhsr')]_p$
and 
$\sigma(x')=w[\sigma(\rhsr')]_p=t'$
for some $p>\toppos$ and rule $\lhsr'\to\rhsr'\IF\gencond'$ such that $\sigma(\gencond')$ holds.
%
By $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinability of $\pi_{\alpha}$, (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak})
is also $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable (and hence $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr/E}$-joinable).
\end{proof}

\subsection{$\cR^\RMabbr,E$-coherence peaks}
\label{SecEPeaksAndLocalCoherence}

Given an \egtrs{} $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ and terms $s$, $t$, $t'$ defining a PS-c-peak (\ref{LblAbstractCPeakJK86}), i.e.,
%
\begin{eqnarray}
t\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E} s\rew{\eqoriented{E}} t'
\label{LblECohPeakTerms}
\end{eqnarray}
%
by Proposition \ref{PropUseOfRulesAndPositionsInRewritingSteps_EGTRSs}(\ref{PropUseOfRulesAndPositionsInRewritingSteps_EGTRSs_PStickel}), 
there are
%
positions $\ol{p},\ol{p'}\in\Pos^\mu(s)$,
%
an \emph{oriented} equation 
$\elhsr\to\erhsr\IF\gencondbis\in\:\eqoriented{E}$,
%
a rule $\alpha:\lhsr\to\rhsr\IF\gencond\in R^\showRMabbr$ (sharing no variables), 
and
substitution $\sigma$,
such that 
(i) $s|_{\ol{p}}=w\equequ{E}\sigma(\lhsr)$ and $\sigma(\gencond)$ hold; 
and 
(ii) $s|_{\ol{p'}}=\sigma(\elhsr)$ and $\sigma(\gencondbis)$ hold,
every coherence peak (\ref{LblECohPeakTerms}) is of the form
\begin{eqnarray}
t = s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}}~ \leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E} ~ s[\underleftarrow{w}]_{\ol{p}}~~=& s & =~~s[\underrightarrow{\sigma(\elhsr)}]_{\ol{p'}} ~\rew{\eqoriented{E}}~
s[\sigma(\erhsr)]_{\ol{p'}}=t'\label{GenericECohPeakRewriting}
\end{eqnarray}
%
Note from Table \ref{TableJoinabilityOfRpeaksJK86}, that PS-c-peaks are required to be $\rsejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable 
(or just $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable if $\cR$ is $E$-terminating).

\subsubsection{Classes of PS-c-peaks}
%
As usual, depending on the relative locations of $\ol{p}$ and $\ol{p'}$, different peaks (\ref{GenericECohPeakRewriting}) are distinguished.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{\emph{Disjoint} PS-c-peaks.} If $\ol{p}$ and $\ol{p'}$ in (\ref{GenericECohPeakRewriting})
are \emph{disjoint},
then $s=s[w]_{\ol{p}}[\sigma(\elhsr)]_{\ol{p'}}=s[\sigma(\elhsr)]_{\ol{p'}}[w]_{\ol{p}}$ and
we have:
\[
t = s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}}[\sigma(\elhsr)]_{\ol{p'}}~\leftrew{\eqoriented{E}}~ 
s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}} [\sigma(\erhsr)]_{\ol{p'}} 
\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}~ s[w]_{\ol{p}}[\sigma(\erhsr)]_{\ol{p'}}  = t'
\]
Since $t ~\rew{\eqoriented{E}}~ 
s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}} [\sigma(\erhsr)]_{\ol{p'}}$ implies $t ~\equequ{E}~ 
s[\sigma(\rhsr)]_{\ol{p}} [\sigma(\erhsr)]_{\ol{p'}}$,
$t$ and $t'$ are  $\rsejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{\emph{Nested} PS-c-peaks.} If $\ol{p}$ and $\ol{p'}$ in (\ref{GenericECohPeakRewriting})
are \emph{not} disjoint,  then (\ref{GenericECohPeakRewriting})
can be written in one of the following three ways (again, by abuse, we use $t$ and $t'$):
\begin{eqnarray}
t = \sigma(\elhsr)[\sigma(\rhsr)]_p ~ \leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E} & \underrightarrow{\overleftarrow{\sigma(\elhsr)}} & \rew{\eqoriented{E}}  ~\sigma(\erhsr)=t'\label{NestedPSCrootPeak}\\
%
t = \sigma(\elhsr)[\sigma(\rhsr)]_p ~ \leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E} & \underrightarrow{\sigma(\elhsr)[\overleftarrow{w}]_p} & \rew{\eqoriented{E}}  ~\sigma(\erhsr)=t'\label{NestedPSCupPeak}\\
%
t =  ~\sigma(\rhsr)\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E} & \overleftarrow{w[\underrightarrow{\sigma(\elhsr)}]_p} & \rew{\eqoriented{E}}  w[\sigma(\erhsr)]_p =t'\label{NestedPSCdownPeak}
\end{eqnarray}
%
that we call PS-c-\emph{root}-peak
 (\ref{NestedPSCrootPeak}),
PS-c-\emph{up}-peak 
(\ref{NestedPSCupPeak}), 
and 
PS-c-\emph{down}-peak 
(\ref{NestedPSCdownPeak}), depending on the 
application of the $\rew{\eqoriented{E}}$-step.
Note that  $\sigma(\lhsr)=_E\sigma(\elhsr)$ in  (\ref{NestedPSCrootPeak}),
%
and $p>\toppos$ in (\ref{NestedPSCupPeak}) and (\ref{NestedPSCdownPeak}).

\begin{proposition}\label{PropJoinabilityOfEdownECohPeaks}
PS-c-root peaks 
(\ref{NestedPSCrootPeak}) and 
PS-c-down peaks (\ref{NestedPSCdownPeak}) 
are 
$\rsjoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable.
\end{proposition}
%
\begin{proof}
For PS-c-root (\ref{NestedPSCrootPeak}) peaks it is obvious.
%
For PS-c-down peaks (\ref{NestedPSCdownPeak}), i.e.,
% 
 \begin{eqnarray}
t =  ~\sigma(\rhsr)\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E} & \overleftarrow{w[\underrightarrow{\sigma(\elhsr)}]_p} & \rew{\eqoriented{E}}  w[\sigma(\erhsr)]_p =t'\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
%
where $w=w[\sigma(\elhsr)]_p =_E \sigma(\lhsr)$, we have $t'\oneconversion{E}w =_E \sigma(\lhsr)\rewAtPos{\toppos}{\alpha}\sigma(\rhsr)=t$. 
%
Therefore,
${t=\sigma(\rhsr)\leftrew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}t'}$, i.e.,
(\ref{NestedPSCdownPeak})
is $\rsjoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable.
\end{proof}
%
As a consequence of this result, as for $\rsejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinability
of PS-c-peaks, \emph{only  PS-c-up peaks (\ref{NestedPSCupPeak}) need to be considered in some detail}. 
%
In this respect, we distinguish two cases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $p\in\Pos^\mu_\Symbols(\elhsr)$, then $\sigma(\elhsr)|_p=\sigma(\elhsr|_p)=w=_E\sigma(\lhsr)$, i.e.,
$\lhsr$ and $\elhsr|_p$ $E$-unify. Then, we say that
 (\ref{NestedPSCupPeak}) is a \emph{critical PS-c-up-peak}; 
%
\item If $p\notin\Pos^\mu_\Symbols(\elhsr)$, there is $x\in\Var^\mu(\elhsr)$ 
and $q\in\Pos^\mu(\elhsr)$ such that $\elhsr|_q=x$ and $q\leq p$.
Then, we say
that  (\ref{NestedPSCupPeak}) is a \emph{variable PS-c-up-peak}.
\end{enumerate}

all conditional pairs in $\LCCP(E,\cR)\cup\CVPofPStickel(E)$ are $\rsejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable (or just $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable, if $\cR$ is $E$-terminating). 
\end{proposition}

As a consequence of Propositions \ref{PropEGTRSsAndLocalCoherenceOfRupEwithR} and  \ref{PropJoinabilityOfCVPsUnconditionalRules}, we have the following.

\begin{corollary}
\label{CoroEGTRSsAndLocalConfluenceModuloEOfRupEwithRleftLinearRules}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an $E$-terminating \egtrs{} such that
all rules in $\eqoriented{E}$ are left-$\mu$-homogeneous and $\mu$-compatible.
%
Then, $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally coherent modulo $E$ iff 
all conditional pairs in $\LCCP(E,\cR)$ 
are $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable.
\end{corollary}

The following result shows how to prove and
disprove $E$-confluence.

\begin{theorem}
\label{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an $\egtrs{}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs_item4} If $\cR$ is $E$-terminating and
every $\pi\in\LCCP(\cR)\cup\CVPofPStickel(\cR)\cup\DCP(\cR)\cup\LCCP(E,\cR)\cup\CVPofPStickel(E)$ is $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable,
 then $\cR$ is $E$-confluent.
 %
\item\label{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs_item5} If there is $\pi\in\LCCP(\cR)\cup\CVPofPStickel(\cR)\cup\DCP(\cR)$ which is \emph{not}
$\cR/E$-joinable, then $\cR$ is not $E$-confluent.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

%
\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}
\item By Proposition \ref{PropEGTRSsAndLocalConfluenceModuloEOfRupEwithR}, 
$\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally confluent modulo $E$.
%
By Proposition \ref{PropEGTRSsAndLocalCoherenceOfRupEwithR}, 
$\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally coherent modulo $E$.
%
Now use Corollary \ref{CoroSufficientCriteriaForEConfluenceOfEGRSs}(\ref{CoroSufficientCriteriaForEConfluenceOfEGRSs_JK86}).
%
\item Since conditional pairs in $\LCCP(\cR)\cup\CVPofPStickel(\cR)\cup\DCP(\cR)$ represent $\peakOf{\cR^\RMabbr,E}{\cR^\RMabbr}$-peaks, the claim follows by Corollary \ref{CoroDisprovingEConcludenceByNonREJoinableLocalConfluencePeaks}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}
%
\begin{example}
\label{ExPeakNoCPs_notEconfluent}
For $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs},
the DCP (\ref{ExPeakNoCPs_DCP2}) 
has been proved non-$\cR/E$-joinable in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_DCPs}.
%
By Theorem \ref{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs}(\ref{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs_item5}), 
$\cR$ is \emph{not} $E$-confluent.
%
Note that $\LCCP(\cR)$ consists of a trivial, hence $\joinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable LCCP (see Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_LCCPs}) 
and
$\CVPofPStickel(\cR)$ is empty (Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_CVPofPStickel}). Thus, $\DCP(\cR)$ is the only 
set of conditional pairs that can be used to disprove $E$-confluence of $\cR$, witnessed by the
PS-r-down critical peak
\begin{eqnarray}
\fS{d}~\leftarrowWith{\cR^\RMabbr,E}   & \fS{f}(\fS{c})  & \rew{\cR^\RMabbr}\fS{f}(\fS{d})
\label{ExPeakNoCPs_PSRDownPeak}
\end{eqnarray}
which is not $\cR/E$-joinable.
\end{example}

In the proof of the following result, as in  Jouannaud and Kirchner's proofs \cite{JouKir_CompletionOfASetOfRulesModuloASetOfEquations_SIAMJC86}, we use \emph{multiset induction} based on a well-founded set $(A,>)$  from which the (possibly repeated) components of the multiset $M$ are obtained. 
%
Given multisets $M$ and $M'$ of elements of $A$, we write $M>M'$ if $M'$ is obtained from $M$ by
\emph{removing} elements from $M$ or by 
\emph{replacing} elements $a\in M$ by other elements
$a_1,\ldots\in A$ such that $a>a_i$ for all $i\geq 1$
\cite{DerMan_ProvingTerminationWithMultisetOrderings_ICALP79}
(see also \cite[Definition 2.3.10]{Ohlebusch_AdvTopicsTermRew_2002}).

\begin{theorem}
\label{TheoEConfluenceWithoutDCPs}
Let $\cR=(\Symbols,\SPredicates,\mu,E,H,R)$ be an $E$-terminating \egtrs{}.
%
If all pairs in $\LCCP(\cR)
\cup
\CVPofPStickel(\cR)\cup\LCCP(E,\cR)\cup\CVPofPStickel(E)
$ are $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable, 
then $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$  has the $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-Church-Rosser property modulo $E$. Thus, it is $E$-confluent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition \ref{PropEGTRSsAndLocalCoherenceOfRupEwithR}, $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally coherent modulo $E$.
%
According to Theorem \ref{TheoTheorem5_JK86}, 
since $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally coherent modulo $E$, 
we prove that $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally coherent modulo $E$ with $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$.
%
Since disjoint PS r-peaks are trivially $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinable,
we consider PS r-up-peaks (\ref{NestedPSRupPeak})
and
PS r-down-peaks (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak}).
%
$\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinability of PS r-up-peaks follows from $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinability of conditional pairs in 
$\LCCP(\cR)
\cup
\CVPofPStickel(\cR)$.
%
Regarding PS r-down-peaks, we write them as follows:
%
\begin{eqnarray}
t =  \sigma(\rhsr')~\leftrewAtPos{\toppos}{\alpha'}\sigma(\lhsr')=w_n\equone{E}\cdots\equone{E} 
w_2\equone{E}w_1=   w[\sigma(\lhsr)]_p \rewAtPos{p}{\alpha}~w[\sigma(\rhsr)]_p=t'
\label{NestedPSRdownPeakDetail}
\end{eqnarray}
%
If $n=0$, then $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinability of $t$ and $t'$ follows from $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinability of $\lccpOf{\alpha',p,\alpha}\in\LCCP(\cR)$.
%
If $n>0$, then 
we prove $\rew{\cR,E}$ locally confluent modulo $E$ with $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$ by multiset induction.
%
Since $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally coherent modulo $E$, from (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeakDetail}), we obtain the following diagram:
\begin{center}
\xymatrix{
w_n\ar@{->}[dd]_{\toppos}^>>{\cR}\ar@{|-|}[rr]_{E}  
& & w_{n-1}\ar@{->}[dd]^>>{\cR,E}
\ar@{|-|}[r]_{E} 
&  \cdots \ar@{|-|}[r]_{E} 
& w_2 \ar@{->}[dd]^>>{\cR,E} \ar@{|-|}[rr]_{E} 
& & w_1\ar@{->}[dd]^>>{\cR,E} \ar@{->}[ddrr]_>>{\alpha}
\\
\\
t \ar@{->}[ddrrr]^{*}_>>{\cR,E} & \ejoinability{\cR,E} & t_{n-1} &  \cdots & t_2 & \ejoinability{\cR,E} & t_1 &\ejoinability{\cR,E} & t'\ar@{->}[ddlll]_{*}^>>{\cR,E}
\\
\\
&& & \nfOf{t}\ar@{|-|}[rr]^{*}_{E} && \nfOf{t'}
}
\end{center}
%
Since the multiset $\{t,t_{n-1},\ldots,t_1,t'\}$ that satisfies $t\oneCRs{} t_{n-1}\oneCRs{}t_{n-2}\oneCRs{} \cdots\oneCRs{} t_1\oneCRs{} t'$ is strictly smaller than $\{w_n,\ldots,w_1\}$
with respect to the well-founded relation $\rew{\cR^\RMabbr/E}$ (due to $E$-termination of $\cR$) and $\rew{\cR,E}\subseteq\rew{\cR/E}$, by the induction hypothesis, we conclude that $t$ and $t'$ are $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable by applying the Church-Rosser property to $t\oneCRs{} t_{n-1}\oneCRs{}t_{n-2}\oneCRs{} \cdots\oneCRs{} t_1\oneCRs{} t'$.
\end{proof}
%
\begin{example}
\label{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_EConfluence}
For $\cR$ and $E$ in Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_EGTRS}, 
%
$\LCCP(E,\cR)=\emptyset$ (Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_LCCPs}) and
%
$\CVPofPStickel(\cR)$ consists of two $\lsejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable CVPs (Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_CVPsOfPStickel}).
%
By Proposition \ref{PropEGTRSsAndLocalCoherenceOfRupEwithR}, 
$\rew{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$ is locally coherent modulo $E$.
Besides,
$\LCCP(\cR)$ consists of a trivial, hence $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinable 
LCCP (Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_LCCPs}) and
%
$\CVPofPStickel(E)$ is empty
(Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818_PSECVPs});
%
By Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceWithoutDCPs}, $\cR$ is $E$-confluent.
\end{example}
%
Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_DCPs} shows that $\cR^\RMabbr,E$-joinability of all $\pi\in\LCCP(\cR)\cup\CVP(\cR)$ does \emph{not} imply $\cR^\RMabbr,E$-joinability
of DCPs in $\DCP(\cR)$ unless the conditions in Proposition \ref{PropJoinabilityOfDCPsAsJoinabilityOfLCCPsAndCVPs} are fulfilled.

\section{Related work}
\label{SecRelatedWork}

\paragraph{Huet.}

Dealing with \emph{left-linear} unconditional rules, 
Huet proved that what we call \emph{variable c-down-peaks} here (\ref{NestedECohPeakRewritingEdown_Huet}) 
are \emph{harmless}  (see Case 2a in the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.5]{Huet_ConfReduc_JACM80}).
%
In our setting, 
Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_EConfluence}) works without assuming left-linearity of rules; 
for \etrs{s} (with no conditional rule or equation, and without replacement restrictions) since $\muTop$ would be used, $\muTop$-homogeneity and $\muTop$-compatibility trivially hold.
Thus,
Corollaries 
\ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForCriticalVariablesNotInCond} and
and \ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks}(\ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks_CVPto}) show that CVPs in $\CVPofR(\cR)$ and $\CVPofR(E)$ are always $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr}$-joinable.
Also, $\muTop$-left-linearity and left-linearity coincide, and hence
Corollary \ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks}(\ref{CoroJoinableVariablePairsForECoherencePeaks_CVPeq})
shows that left-linearity can be seen as a sufficient condition for $\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr}$-joinablity of CVPs in $\CVPofEqOne(\cR)$.
%
Actually, Corollary \ref{CoroEConfluenceOfETerminatingLeftLinearEGTRSsHuet} and \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Huet_ConfReduc_JACM80} \emph{coincide} 
if the $\egtrs{}$
in Corollary \ref{CoroEConfluenceOfETerminatingLeftLinearEGTRSsHuet} 
is obtained from an
\etrs{}
consisting of 
a set $E$ of 
(unconditional) equations and
a set $R$ of 
\emph{left-linear} (unconditional) rules such that
$\cR$ is $E$-terminating, as required in \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Huet_ConfReduc_JACM80}:
%
Huet's result implies $E$-confluence of $\cR$ if all critical pairs in 
$\CP(\cR)\cup\CP(E,\cR)\cup\CP(\cR,E)$ are $\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinable.
%
In this case, such (unconditional) critical pairs coincide with 
$\CCP(\cR)\cup\CCP(E,\cR)\cup\CCP(\cR,E)$.
%
Thus, Corollary \ref{CoroEConfluenceOfETerminatingLeftLinearEGTRSsHuet} applies to conclude $E$-confluence of $\cR$.

Furthermore, $E$-confluence of the \trs{} $\cR$ 
in Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818variant} 
cannot be proved by using \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Huet_ConfReduc_JACM80}, as $\cR$ is not left-linear.
%
However, we could prove it using our methods (Example \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818variant_EConfluence}).

\paragraph{Jouannaud and Kirchner.}
 
The main result for ETRSs 
\cite[Theorem 16]{JouKir_CompletionOfASetOfRulesModuloASetOfEquations_SIAMJC86},
cannot be used to \emph{disprove} $E$-confluence of ETRSs
as the theorem proves the $\rew{\cR,E}$-Church-Rosser property, which is only a sufficient condition for $E$-confluence.
%
For instance, for $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs}, the proof of non-$E$-confluence in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_notEconfluent} would not be obtained.
%
Actually, (\ref{ExPeakNoCPs_PSRDownPeak})  in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs_notEconfluent} 
is a PS-r-down peak (\ref{NestedPSRdownPeak}). 
%
Such peaks are explictly \emph{excluded} to obtain $E$-critical pairs in
\cite{Jouannaud_ConfluentAndCoherentEquationalTermRewritingSystemsApplicationToProofsInAbstractDataTypes_CAAP83,JouKir_CompletionOfASetOfRulesModuloASetOfEquations_SIAMJC86}\footnote{\emph{``we do not consider the case where $\rew{\cR}$ applies at an occurrence $p$ and $\rew{\cR,E}$ at the outermost occurrence $\toppos$''} \cite[below $E$-critical pairs lemma]{JouKir_CompletionOfASetOfRulesModuloASetOfEquations_SIAMJC86} (notation adapted).}. 
%
Our \emph{down conditional pairs} (DCPs) fill this gap. 

On the other hand, Jouannaud and Kirchner's results 
permit the particularization of $\genrelationUpE$ to the combination
$\rew{\cL}\cup\rew{\cN,E}$ of rewriting and Peterson \& Stickel rewriting, 
where $\cL$ and $\cN$ partition $\cR$ into a left-linear system $\cL$,
and $\cN$ which
includes any (possibly left-linear) rule not in $\cL$ \cite[Section 3.5]{JouKir_CompletionOfASetOfRulesModuloASetOfEquations_SIAMJC86}.

The case considered here, where $\genrelationUpE$ is 
$\rew{\cR,E}$, is a particular case of the previous one, where $\cL=\emptyset$ and $\cN=\cR$.
%
Under these conditions, \cite[Theorem 16]{JouKir_CompletionOfASetOfRulesModuloASetOfEquations_SIAMJC86}, as sufficient $E$-confluence criterion,
boils down to Theorem 
\ref{TheoEConfluenceWithoutDCPs}.
This is because \etrs{s} consist of unconditional rules and no replacement restriction is considered. Thus, rules are trivially left-$\muTop$-homogeneous and $\muTop$-compatible. Therefore, by Propositions \ref{CoroJoinableVariablePSrUpPeaksForCriticalVariablesNotInCondition} 
and \ref{PropJoinabilityOfCVPsUnconditionalRules} 
all CVPs in $\CVPofPStickel(\cR)$ and 
$\CVPofPStickel(E)$ are $\joinability{\cR,E}$-joinable and can be dismissed. 

The aforementioned more general treatment for \egtrs{s} where $\genrelationUpE$ is
$\rew{\cL}\cup\rew{\cN,E}$ is left as an interesting subject for future work.

\paragraph{Dur\'an and Meseguer.}

The $E$-confluence of 
\emph{conditional rewrite theories} $\cR=(\Symbols,E,R)$ has been investigated in \cite{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}.
%
Conditional equations $s=t\IF\gencond$
can be specified, but they are treated as conditional
rewrite rules (in $R$) by imposing some specific orientation 
(e.g., $s\to t\IF\gencond$). Only unconditional equations $s=t$ 
(called \emph{axioms})  which are
\emph{linear} and \emph{regular} (i.e., $\Var(s)=\Var(t)$
\cite[page 819]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12})
are used in $E$ (denoted $A$ in \cite{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}).

The main result about $E$-confluence is \cite[Theorem 2]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}, characterizing $E$-confluence 
as the $\joinability{\cR,A}$-joinability (\cite[Definition 7]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}) of the set of 
\emph{Equational Conditional Critical Pairs} 
with respect to the equational theory 
$A$ (see Section \ref{SecECCPsAndLCTRS}) 
obtained (if an appropriate $A$-unification algorithm exists) from rules 
in $R$ (which may include oriented conditional equations). 
%
However, a number of restrictions are imposed \cite[Section 3.1]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
$A$ is a set of \emph{linear and regular unconditional} equations;
\item 
$R$ is \emph{strongly $A$-coherent}, i.e., the following diagram commutes
\cite[page 819]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}:
\begin{xy}
\xymatrix{
 u  \ar@{->}[rr]_{\cR/A}  \ar@{|-|}[d]_{*}^{A} & & v\ar@{|.|}[d]^{*}_{A} 
\\
u' \ar@{.>}[rr]_{\cR,A} & & v'
}
\end{xy}

\item 
the rules in $R$ are \emph{strongly deterministic} \cite[Definition 1]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12};
and
\item 
$\cR$ is \emph{quasi-decreasing} \cite[Definition 2]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}, which is quite a strong termination condition. Together with strong $A$-coherence above, it entails $E$-termination.
\end{enumerate}
Such criteria, in particular quasi-decreasingness, can be used to decide the appropriate orientation of equations in $E$ into rules to be added to $R$.
%
By lack of space, we cannot provide a detailed comparison with our approach. However, sometimes our results can be advantageously used to improve on \cite{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}:
%
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$E$-confluence of $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExRModuloAndRrelativeE}
cannot be proved with \cite[Theorem 2]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12} as $\cR$ is \emph{not} strongly deterministic \cite[Definition 1]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}: condition $\fS{b}\rews{}\fS{c}$ in rule (\ref{ExRModuloAndRrelativeE_rule2})
does not fulfill the requirement of $\rew{\cR,E}$-irreducibility of $\fS{c}$. 
%
We prove $E$-confluence of $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExRModuloAndRrelativeE_EConfluence}.
\item 
\cite[Theorem 2]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12} would \emph{not} apply to disprove $E$-confluence of 
$\cR$ in Example \ref{ExPeakNoCPs};
%
note that $E$ satisfies the requirements for axioms $A$ in \cite{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12}.
%
We have:
$\fS{b}\equequ{E}\fS{f}(\ul{\fS{a}})\rew{\cR}\fS{f}(\fS{d})$, i.e., $\fS{b}\rew{\cR/E}\fS{f}(\fS{d})$,
but the only $\rew{\cR,E}$-step on $\fS{b}$ is $\fS{b}\rew{\cR,E}\fS{d}$, and
$\fS{f}(\fS{d})\neq_E\fS{d}$. Thus, $\cR$ is not strongly $E$-coherent
and \cite[Theorem 2]{DurMes_OnTheChurchRosserAndCoherencePropertiesOfConditionalOrderSortedRewriteTheories_JLAP12} does not apply.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Meseguer.}

Coherence of conditional rewriting modulo axioms is investigated in
\cite{Meseguer_StrictCoherenceOfConditionalRewritingModuloAxioms_TCS17}.
%
Working on Jouannaud and Kirchner's abstract approach, in \cite[Section 4.3]{Meseguer_StrictCoherenceOfConditionalRewritingModuloAxioms_TCS17}
the problem discussed in Example \ref{ExRModuloAndRrelativeE} is noticed.
That is: in conditional rewriting,
%
%Thus, 
the \emph{natural choice} of 
interpreting 
$\genrelation$ as $\rew{\cR}$,
$\genequivalence$ as $\equequ{E}$, 
and $\genrelation/\genequivalence$ as $\rew{\cR/E}$ does \emph{not} fulfill the requirement (\ref{LblReductionModuloFromReductionAndEquivalence}) of Jouannaud and Kirchner's abstract framework, i.e.,  $\rew{\cR/E}$ and $\composeRel{\equequ{E}}{\composeRel{\rew{\cR}}{\equequ{E}}}$ does \emph{not} coincide.
%
Meseguer's solution is interpreting
$\genrelation$ and $\genrelationUpE$ as the \emph{same} relation, see
\cite[paragraph above Proposition 1]{Meseguer_StrictCoherenceOfConditionalRewritingModuloAxioms_TCS17}.
%
This solution, though, is not appropriate for our purposes, as it implies that only 
$\leftrew{\cR,E}\circ\rew{\cR,E}$ and $\leftrew{\cR,E}\circ\equone{E}$ peaks can be considered,
thus making the use of $E$-unification mandatory when computing CCPs.
%
In contrast, our approach also permits $E$-confluence proofs based on considering ``classical'' conditional critical pairs, not requiring $E$-unifiers,
as in Sections \ref{SecAnalysisOfRandCpeaks}
and \ref{SecEConfluenceWithRandCpeaks}.

\renewcommand{\RMabbr}{\mathit{rm}}

\section{Conclusion and future work}
\label{SecConclusionAndFutureWork}

We have introduced \emph{Equational Generalized Term Rewriting Systems} (\egtrs{s})
consisting of \emph{conditional rules}  
and \emph{conditional equations} 
whose conditions are sequences of \emph{atoms}, possibly defined by
additional Horn clauses.
%
Replacement restrictions $\mu$ specifying which arguments of function symbols can be rewritten are also allowed.
%
Rewriting computations with \egtrs{s} $\cR$ 
are described by \emph{deduction} in 
appropriate First-Order theories.

We have shown that an appropriate definition of a rewrite relation 
$\rew{\cR^\RMabbr}$ based on a modification of the treatment of the conditional part of clauses in $H$ and $R$ permits the use of Jouannaud and Kirchner's framework in Section \ref{SecBasicNotionsJK86}
to prove $E$-confluence of \egtrs{s} (Table \ref{TableARSsAndEGTRSs}).
%
As discussed in Section \ref{SecRelatedWork}, when 
compared to related uses of the framework
(e.g., in \cite{Meseguer_StrictCoherenceOfConditionalRewritingModuloAxioms_TCS17}), our approach permits a more flexible application of Jouannaud and Kirchner's framework to conditional rewriting.

We have shown that $E$-confluence of $E$-terminating  
\egtrs{s} can be 
\emph{proved} 
by checking 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\ejoinability{\cR}$-joinability of 
(i) CCPs in $\CCP(\cR)$ and CVPs in $\CVPofR(\cR)$ 
representing
local confluence peaks $\peakOf{\cR}{\cR}$ using $\rew{\cR}$ to build the 
fork,
and 
(ii) CCPs in $\CCP(E,\cR)$ and $\CCP(\cR,E)$ and
CVPs in $\CVPofR(E)$ and $\CVPofEqOne(\cR)$ representing
local coherence peaks $\peakOf{\cR}{E}$ using $\rew{\cR}$ and $\rew{\eqoriented{E}}$ (see Table \ref{TableConditionalPairsForPeaksHuet} and Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_EConfluence})), 
and also
%
\item $\ejoinability{\cR,E}$-joinability of 
(i) LCCPs in $\LCCP(\cR)$ and CVPs in $\CVPofPStickel(\cR)$, and DCPs in $\DCP(\cR)$ representing
local confluence peaks $\peakOf{\cR,E}{\cR}$ using $\rew{\cR,E}$ and $\rew{\cR}$ 
to build the fork,
and 
(ii) LCCPs in $\LCCP(E,\cR)$ and CVPs in $\CVPofPStickel(E)$ 
representing local coherence peaks $\peakOf{\cR,E}{E}$ using $\rew{\cR,E}$ and $\rew{\eqoriented{E}}$
(Table \ref{TableConditionalPairsForPeaks} and Theorems \ref{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs}(\ref{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs_item4}) and \ref{TheoEConfluenceWithoutDCPs}).
\end{enumerate}
%
We provide criteria for disproving $E$-confluence on the basis of the non-$\ejoinability{\cR/E}$-joinability of conditional pairs as the aforementioned ones 
(Theorems \ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet}(\ref{TheoEConfluenceOfETerminatingEGTRSsHuet_NonEConfluent}) and 
\ref{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs}(\ref{TheoremEConfluenceOfEGRSs_item5})).

Although CCPs and CVPs were already used in proofs of confluence of \gtrs{s}, here CCPs are used not only to deal with overlaps between rules of $R^\RMabbr$ but also to handle overlaps between rules from $R^\RMabbr$ 
and $\eqoriented{E}$.
%
Furthermore, we have introduced 
the notion of \emph{parametric} CVP, which are used in several novel ways specific for proving $E$-confluence, as in the definitions of 
$\CVPofR(E)$, $\CVPofEqOne(\cR)$, $\CVPofPStickel(\cR)$, and $\CVPofPStickel(E)$.
%
Besides, DCPs have been introduced here and showed useful to \emph{disprove} $E$-confluence, although can also be dismissed under some conditions (Theorem \ref{TheoEConfluenceWithoutDCPs}).
%
Finally, we have also introduced LCCPs as an alternative to ECCPs to 
avoid the computation of $E$-unifiers in proofs of $E$-confluence, thus leading to a finite representation of local confluence and coherence peaks $\peakOf{\cR,E}{\cR}$ and $\peakOf{\cR,E}{E}$.
As far as we know, CVPs, DCPs, and LCCPs 
have not been used yet  in proofs of $E$-confluence.

The discussed examples (see also Section \ref{SecRelatedWork})
show that the new techniques are useful, not only for \egtrs{s} which cannot be seen as already existing rewriting-based systems (for instance, $\cR$ in Examples \ref{ExSumListsA} and \ref{ExEvenEq}), 
but also for those which can be seen as \etrs{s} (e.g., $\cR$ in Examples \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818}, \ref{ExPeakNoCPs}, and \ref{ExHuet80_RemarkPage818variant}) 
or conditional rewrite theories (e.g., $\cR$ in Example \ref{ExRModuloAndRrelativeE}) as existing results cannot 
appropriately handle them.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Future work.} Much work remains to be done for a \emph{practical} use of these new proposals.

First, $E$-termination of \egtrs{s} $\cR$, which is required in our main results, is underexplored to date.
%
As discussed in Section  \ref{SecETerminationOfEGTRSs}, the 
(automatic) computation of models of $\GLtheory_{\cR/E}$ 
making $\rewmodulo{}$ well-founded is possible by using existing tools (e.g., \AGES{} or \MaceFour{}) is an interesting starting point, but
the development of more specific techniques would be necessary.

Also, our results
heavily rely on checking 
$\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr}$-joinability,
$\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr,E}$-joinability and
non-$\ejoinability{\cR^\RMabbr/E}$-joinability of 
CCPs, (different kinds of) CVPs, DCPs, and  LCCPs to obtain proofs of (non)
$E$-confluence.
%
We plan to improve our tool \CONFident{} \cite{GutLucVit_ProvingConfluenceInTheConfluenceFrameworkWithCONFident_FI24}, 
which 
implements methods for the  analysis of similar conditional pairs. 
%
Such results heavily relies on the (in)feasibility results developed in \cite{GutLuc_AutomaticallyProvingAndDisprovingFeasibilityConditions_IJCAR20} and 
implemented in the tool \infChecker{}, which currently deals with \csctrs{s} and
should also be adapted to deal with more general thories as the ones used with \egtrs{s}.
%
\infChecker{} also uses theorem provers like \ProverNine{} \cite{McCune_Prove9andMace4_Unpublished10}
and model generators like \MaceFour{}  
and \AGES{} 
to implement these checkings.
%
Overall, this approach has proved useful to prove confluence of 
variants of TRSs,
see \cite[Section 8]{GutLucVit_ProvingConfluenceInTheConfluenceFrameworkWithCONFident_FI24}
for an account.
%
Also, from a practical point of view, 
it is important to investigate the possibility 
of a \emph{mixed} use of ECCPs
together 
with LCCPs.
%
For instance, if there is an $E$-unification algorithm and the set of (complete) 
$E$-unifiers is finite, then the corresponding (computable and finite set of) 
ECCPs could be used instead 
of LCCPs.

Finally, exploring the impact of our techniques in \emph{first-order deduction modulo} see, e.g., \cite{Dowek_AutomatedTheoremProvingInFirstOrderLogicModuloOnTheDifferenceBetweenTypeTheoryAndSetTheory_arXiv23} and the references therein, 
is another interesting subject of future work.

title: LDP$^3$: An Extensible and Multi-Threaded Toolkit for Local Differential Privacy Protocols and Post-Processing Methods
summary:
Local differential privacy (LDP) has become a prominent notion for
privacy-preserving data collection. While numerous LDP protocols and
post-processing (PP) methods have been developed, selecting an optimal
combination under different privacy budgets and datasets remains a challenge.
Moreover, the lack of a comprehensive and extensible LDP benchmarking toolkit
raises difficulties in evaluating new protocols and PP methods. To address
these concerns, this paper presents LDP$^3$ (pronounced LDP-Cube), an
open-source, extensible, and multi-threaded toolkit for LDP researchers and
practitioners. LDP$^3$ contains implementations of several LDP protocols, PP
methods, and utility metrics in a modular and extensible design. Its modular
design enables developers to conveniently integrate new protocols and PP
methods. Furthermore, its multi-threaded nature enables significant reductions
in execution times via parallelization. Experimental evaluations demonstrate
that: (i) using LDP$^3$ to select a good protocol and post-processing method
substantially improves utility compared to a bad or random choice, and (ii) the
multi-threaded design of LDP$^3$ brings substantial benefits in terms of
efficiency.

title: Towards Benchmarking Foundation Models for Tabular Data With Text
summary:
Foundation models for tabular data are rapidly evolving, with increasing
interest in extending them to support additional modalities such as free-text
features. However, existing benchmarks for tabular data rarely include textual
columns, and identifying real-world tabular datasets with semantically rich
text features is non-trivial. We propose a series of simple yet effective
ablation-style strategies for incorporating text into conventional tabular
pipelines. Moreover, we benchmark how state-of-the-art tabular foundation
models can handle textual data by manually curating a collection of real-world
tabular datasets with meaningful textual features. Our study is an important
step towards improving benchmarking of foundation models for tabular data with
text.

title: A Frequentist Simulation-Based Inference Treatment of Sterile Neutrino Global Fits
summary:
A critical challenge in particle physics is combining results from diverse
experimental setups that measure the same physical quantity to enhance
precision and statistical power, a process known as a global fit. Global fits
of sterile neutrino searches, hunts for additional neutrino oscillation
frequencies and amplitudes, present an intriguing case study. In such a
scenario, the key assumptions underlying Wilks' theorem, a cornerstone of most
classic frequentist analyses, do not hold. The method of Feldman and Cousins, a
trials-based approach which does not assume Wilks' theorem, becomes
computationally prohibitive for complex or intractable likelihoods. To bypass
this limitation, we borrow a technique from simulation-based inference (SBI) to
estimate likelihood ratios for use in building trials-based confidence
intervals, speeding up test statistic evaluations by a factor $>10^4$ per grid
point, resulting in a faster, but approximate, frequentist fitting framework.
Applied to a subset of sterile neutrino search data involving the disappearance
of muon-flavor (anti)neutrinos, our method leverages machine learning to
compute frequentist confidence intervals while significantly reducing
computational expense. In addition, the SBI-based approach holds additional
value by recognizing underlying systematic uncertainties that the Wilks
approach does not. Thus, our method allows for more robust machine
learning-based analyses critical to performing accurate but computationally
feasible global fits. This allows, for the first time, a global fit to sterile
neutrino data without assuming Wilks' theorem. While we demonstrate the utility
of such a technique studying sterile neutrino searches, it is applicable to
both single-experiment and global fits of all kinds.

bib.abstract: We introduce a new amortized likelihood ratio estimator for likelihood-free simulation-based inference (SBI). Our estimator is simple to train and estimates the likelihood ratio using a single forward pass of the neural estimator. Our approach directly computes the likelihood ratio between two competing parameter sets, which differs from the previous approach of comparing two neural network output values. We refer to our model as the direct neural ratio estimator (DNRE). As part of introducing the DNRE, we derive a corresponding Monte Carlo estimate of the posterior. We benchmark our new ratio estimator and compare it to ratio estimators in the current literature. We show that our new ratio estimator often outperforms these previous approaches. As a further contribution, we introduce a new derivative estimator for likelihood ratio estimators that enables us to compare likelihood-free Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with random-walk Metropolis-Hastings (MH). We show that HMC is equally competitive, which has not been previously shown. Finally, we include a novel real-world application of SBI using our neural ratio estimator to design a quadcopter. Code is available at https://github.com/SRI-CSL/dnre.
bib.title: Direct amortized likelihood ratio estimation

bib.abstract: This article reports global fits of short-baseline neutrino data to oscillation models involving light sterile neutrinos. In the commonly-used 3+1 plane wave model, there is a well-known 4.9$\sigma$ tension between data sets sensitive to appearance versus disappearance of neutrinos. We find that models that damp the oscillation prediction for the reactor data sets, especially at low energy, substantially improve the fits and reduce the tension. We consider two such scenarios. The first scenario introduces the quantum mechanical wavepacket effect that accounts for the source size in reactor experiments into the 3+1 model. We find that inclusion of the wavepacket effect greatly improves the overall fit compared to a three-neutrino model by ∆$\chi$2/dof = 61.1/4 (7.1$\sigma$ improvement) with best-fit ∆m2 = 1.4 eV2 and wavepacket length of 67 fm. The internal tension is reduced to 3.4$\sigma$. If reactor-data only is fit, then the wavepacket preferred length is 91 fm (> 20 fm at 99{\%} CL). The second model introduces oscillations involving sterile flavor and allows the decay of the heaviest, mostly sterile mass state, $\nu$4. This model introduces a damping term similar to the wavepacket effect, but across all experiments. Compared to a three-neutrino fit, this has a ∆$\chi$2/dof = 60.6/4 (7$\sigma$ improvement) with preferred ∆m2 = 1.4 eV2 and decay $\Gamma$ = 0.35 eV. The internal tension is reduced to 3.7$\sigma$.
bib.title: New Clues about light sterile neutrinos: preference for models with damping effects in global fits

bib.abstract: This article presents a simulation-based method designed to establish the computational correctness of software developed to fit a specific Bayesian model, capitalizing on properties of Bayesian posterior distributions. We illustrate the validation technique with two examples. The validation method is shown to find errors in software when they exist and, moreover, the validation output can be informative about the nature and location of such errors. We also compare our method with that of an earlier approach.

The problem of testing statistical hypotheses is an old one. Its
origin is usually connected with the name of Thomas Bayes, who
gave the well-known theorem on the probabilities a posteriori of
the possible ``causes`` of a given event. Since then it has been
discussed by many writers of whom we shall here mention two
only, Bertrand and Borel, whose differing views serve well to
illustrate the point from which we shall approach the subject.
Bertrand put into statistical form a variety of hypotheses, as
for example the hypothesis that a given group of stars with
relatively small angular distances between them as seen from the
earth, form a ``system'' or group in space. His method of
attack, which is that in common use, consisted essentially in
calculating the probability, P, that a certain character, x , of
the observed facts would arise if the hypothesis tested were
true. If P were very small, this would generally be considered
as an indication that the hypothesis, H, was probably false, and
vice versa . Bertrand expressed the pessimistic view that no
test of this kind could give reliable results. Borel, however,
in a later discussion, considered that the method described
could be applied with success provided that the character, x ,
of the observed facts were properly chosen---were, in fact, a
character which he terms ``en quelque sorte remarquable.''

bib.abstract: Many domains of science have developed complex simulations to describe phenomena of interest. While these simulations provide high-fidelity models, they are poorly suited for inference and lead to challenging inverse problems. We review the rapidly developing field of simulation-based inference and identify the forces giving additional momentum to the field. Finally, we describe how the frontier is expanding so that a broad audience can appreciate the profound influence these developments may have on science.

bib.abstract:
We propose a new method for approximate Bayesian statistical
inference on the basis of summary statistics. The method is
suited to complex problems that arise in population genetics,
extending ideas developed in this setting by earlier authors.
Properties of the posterior distribution of a parameter, such as
its mean or density curve, are approximated without explicit
likelihood calculations. This is achieved by fitting a
local-linear regression of simulated parameter values on
simulated summary statistics, and then substituting the observed
summary statistics into the regression equation. The method
combines many of the advantages of Bayesian statistical
inference with the computational efficiency of methods based on
summary statistics. A key advantage of the method is that the
nuisance parameters are automatically integrated out in the
simulation step, so that the large numbers of nuisance
parameters that arise in population genetics problems can be
handled without difficulty. Simulation results indicate
computational and statistical efficiency that compares favorably
with those of alternative methods previously proposed in the
literature. We also compare the relative efficiency of
inferences obtained using methods based on summary statistics
with those obtained directly from the data using MCMC.

title: README: Robust Error-Aware Digital Signature Framework via Deep Watermarking Model
summary:
Deep learning-based watermarking has emerged as a promising solution for
robust image authentication and protection. However, existing models are
limited by low embedding capacity and vulnerability to bit-level errors, making
them unsuitable for cryptographic applications such as digital signatures,
which require over 2048 bits of error-free data. In this paper, we propose
README (Robust Error-Aware Digital Signature via Deep WaterMarking ModEl), a
novel framework that enables robust, verifiable, and error-tolerant digital
signatures within images. Our method combines a simple yet effective
cropping-based capacity scaling mechanism with ERPA (ERror PAinting Module), a
lightweight error correction module designed to localize and correct bit errors
using Distinct Circular Subsum Sequences (DCSS). Without requiring any
fine-tuning of existing pretrained watermarking models, README significantly
boosts the zero-bit-error image rate (Z.B.I.R) from 1.2% to 86.3% when
embedding 2048-bit digital signatures into a single image, even under
real-world distortions. Moreover, our use of perceptual hash-based signature
verification ensures public verifiability and robustness against tampering. The
proposed framework unlocks a new class of high-assurance applications for deep
watermarking, bridging the gap between signal-level watermarking and
cryptographic security.

bib.abstract: Steganography is a data hiding technique that is widely used in various information securing applications. Steganography transmits data by hiding the existence of the message so that a viewer cannot identify the transmission of message and hence not able to decrypt it. This work proposes a data securing technique that is used for hiding multiple color images into a single color image using the Discrete Wavelet Transform. The cover image is split up into R, G and B planes. Secret images are embedded into these planes. An N-level decomposition of the cover image and the secret images are done and some frequency components of the same are combined. Secret images are then extracted from the stego image. Here, the stego image obtained has a less perceptible changes compared to the original image with high overall security.

bib.abstract: The advances in computer technologies and the Internet have made rapid strides and breakthroughs in the field of data communication, which nowadays, is easily accessed. Unfortunately, this easy access offers almost endless opportunities for pirating copyrighted and confidential medical imagery. Many methods are proposed in the literature, however, most of them lack in robustness and perceptibility, and are prone to attacks. Hence, this study proposes a robust image steganographic approach that combines Redundant Integer Wavelet Transform (RIWT), Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DCT) and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and the logistic chaotic map. RIWT being a shift invariant, reversibility and robustness were achieved in this proposed technique. Better level of imperceptibility was achieved using SVD and DCT, with embedding carried out on singular values. Extra security was provided using the logistic chaotic map for encryption of secret medical images, which also enhanced the robustness of the technique. bib.abstract: In this paper, a robust blind image watermarking method is proposed for copyright protection of digital images. This hybrid method relies on combining two well-known transforms that are the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and the discrete cosine transform (DCT). The motivation behind this combination is to enhance the imperceptibility and the robustness. The imperceptibility requirement is achieved by using magnitudes of DFT coefficients while the robustness improvement is ensured by applying DCT to the DFT coefficients magnitude. The watermark is embedded by modifying the coefficients of the middle band of the DCT using a secret key. The security of the proposed method is enhanced by applying Arnold transform (AT) to the watermark before embedding. Experiments were conducted on natural and textured images. Results show that, compared with state-of-the-art methods, the proposed method is robust to a wide range of attacks while preserving high imperceptibility.

bib.abstract: An encryption method is presented with the novel property that publicly revealing an encryption key does not thereby reveal the corresponding decryption key. This has two important consequences: (1) Couriers or other secure means are not needed to transmit keys, since a message can be enciphered using an encryption key publicly revealed by the intented recipient. Only he can decipher the message, since only he knows the corresponding decryption key. (2) A message can be “signed” using a privately held decryption key. Anyone can verify this signature using the corresponding publicly revealed encryption key. Signatures cannot be forged, and a signer cannot later deny the validity of his signature. This has obvious applications in “electronic mail” and “electronic funds transfer” systems. A message is encrypted by representing it as a number M, raising M to a publicly specified power e, and then taking the remainder when the result is divided by the publicly specified product, n, of two large secret primer numbers p and q. Decryption is similar; only a different, secret, power d is used, where e * d ≡ 1(mod (p - 1) * (q - 1)). The security of the system rests in part on the difficulty of factoring the published divisor, n.
bib.title: A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems

bib.abstract: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is the elliptic curve analogue of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA). It was accepted in 1999 as an ANSI standard and in 2000 as IEEE and NIST standards. It was also accepted in 1998 as an ISO standard and is under consideration for inclusion in some other ISO standards. Unlike the ordinary discrete logarithm problem and the integer factorization problem, no subexponential-time algorithm is known for the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. For this reason, the strength-per-key-bit is substantially greater in an algorithm that uses elliptic curves. This paper describes the ANSI X9.62 ECDSA, and discusses related security, implementation, and interoperability issues.

title: Iterated jump noncomputability and compactness
summary:
We use reverse mathematics to analyze "iterated jump" versions of the
following four principles: the atomic model theorem with subenumerable types
(AST), the diagonally noncomputable principle (DNR), weak weak K\H{o}nig's
lemma (WWKL), and weak K\H{o}nig's lemma (WKL). The logical relationships
between these principles are summarized in Figure 1 and include, among other
things, an infinite chain and an infinite antichain, the latter of which
represents a strong form of non-linearity in terms of provability strength
among "natural" combinatorial principles.

title: General Molecular Communication Model in Multi-Layered Spherical Channels
summary:
Spherical multi-layered structures are prevalent in numerous biological
systems and engineered applications, including tumor spheroids, layered
tissues, and multi-shell nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery. Despite
their widespread occurrence, there remains a gap in modeling particle
propagation through these complex structures from a molecular communication
(MC) perspective. This paper introduces a generalized analytical framework for
modeling diffusion-based molecular communication in multi-layered spherical
environments. The framework is capable of supporting an arbitrary number of
layers and flexible transmitter-receiver positioning. As an example, the
detailed formulation is presented for the three-layer sphere, which is
particularly relevant for different biological models such as tumor spheroids.
The analytical results are validated using particle-based simulation (PBS) in
scenarios that have short inter-layer distances. The findings reveal that the
characteristics of each layer significantly impact molecule propagation
throughout the entire structure, making their consideration crucial for
designing targeted therapies and optimizing drug delivery systems.

bib.keywords: Receivers;Mathematical model;Channel models;Tutorials;Molecular communication (telecommunication);Diffusion;Nanobioscience;Biological system modeling;Drug delivery;Diffusion;end-to-end channel impulse response (CIR);experiment-driven models;flow;molecular communications (MCs);reaction;simulation-driven models;statistical model
bib.abstract: Molecular communication (MC) is a new communication engineering paradigm where molecules are employed as information carriers. MC systems are expected to enable new revolutionary applications, such as sensing of target substances in biotechnology, smart drug delivery in medicine, and monitoring of oil pipelines or chemical reactors in industrial settings. As for any other kind of communication, simple yet sufficiently accurate channel models are needed for the design, analysis, and efficient operation of MC systems. In this paper, we provide a tutorial review on mathematical channel modeling for diffusive MC systems. The considered end-to-end MC channel models incorporate the effects of the release mechanism, the MC environment, and the reception mechanism on the observed information molecules. Thereby, the various existing models for the different components of an MC system are presented under a common framework and the underlying biological, chemical, and physical phenomena are discussed. Deterministic models characterizing the expected number of molecules observed at the receiver and statistical models characterizing the actual number of observed molecules are developed. In addition, we provide the channel models for time-varying MC systems with moving transmitters and receivers, which are relevant for advanced applications such as smart drug delivery with mobile nanomachines. For complex scenarios, where simple MC channel models cannot be obtained from first principles, we investigate the simulation- and experiment-driven channel models. Finally, we provide a detailed discussion of potential challenges, open research problems, and future directions in channel modeling for diffusive MC systems.
bib.title: Channel Modeling for Diffusive Molecular Communication—A Tutorial Review
bib.author: Jamali, Vahid and Ahmadzadeh, Arman and Wicke, Wayan and Noel, Adam and Schober, Robert

bib.abstract: With much advancement in the field of nanotechnology, bioengineering, and synthetic biology over the past decade, microscales and nanoscales devices are becoming a reality. Yet the problem of engineering a reliable communication system between tiny devices is still an open problem. At the same time, despite the prevalence of radio communication, there are still areas where traditional electromagnetic waves find it difficult or expensive to reach. Points of interest in industry, cities, and medical applications often lie in embedded and entrenched areas, accessible only by ventricles at scales too small for conventional radio waves and microwaves, or they are located in such a way that directional high frequency systems are ineffective. Inspired by nature, one solution to these problems is molecular communication (MC), where chemical signals are used to transfer information. Although biologists have studied MC for decades, it has only been researched for roughly 10 year from a communication engineering lens. Significant number of papers have been published to date, but owing to the need for interdisciplinary work, much of the results are preliminary. In this survey, the recent advancements in the field of MC engineering are highlighted. First, the biological, chemical, and physical processes used by an MC system are discussed. This includes different components of the MC transmitter and receiver, as well as the propagation and transport mechanisms. Then, a comprehensive survey of some of the recent works on MC through a communication engineering lens is provided. The survey ends with a technology readiness analysis of MC and future research directions.

bib.abstract: The purpose of this review is to provide a comprehensive overview of mathematical procedures that can be used to describe the release of drugs from inert matrix systems. The review focuses on general principles rather than particular applications. The inherent multiscale nature of the drug-release process is pointed out and multiscale modelling is exemplified for inert porous matrices. Although effects of stagnant layers and finite volumes of release media are briefly discussed, the systematic analysis is restricted to systems under sink conditions. When the initial drug loading exceeds the drug solubility in the matrix, Higuchi-type moving-boundary descriptions continue to be highly valuable for obtaining approximate analytical solutions, especially when coupled with integral balance methods. Continuous-field descriptions have decisive advantages when numerical solutions are sought. This is because the mathematical formulation reduces to a diffusion equation with a nonlinear source term, valid over the entire matrix domain. Solutions can thus be effortlessly determined for arbitrary geometries using standard numerical packages.
